items.title: I can name the two major divisions of the nervous system and describe what each comprises
items.what: The central nervous system (CNS) comprises the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) comprises every neuron in the body outside the CNS. Together, these two divisions make up the entire nervous system.
items.why: Distinguishing between the CNS and PNS is essential for accurately describing the pathway of neural messages in both conscious and unconscious responses, and is tested directly in VCE exam questions.
items.example: When a person feels cold water on their hand, sensory receptors in the skin (PNS) detect the sensation and send a message toward the brain (CNS) for processing.

subtopic.name: Structure of the Nervous System
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the two major divisions of the nervous system — the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system — and their subdivisions, including the somatic nervous system, autonomic nervous system, sympathetic nervous system, and parasympathetic nervous system. It also covers the three types of neurons and the structures they make up.
subtopic.why: Understanding the structure of the nervous system is the foundation for explaining how the body detects, processes, and responds to information. Every other concept in this chapter depends on knowing which division does what and where.

items.title: I can describe the roles of the brain and spinal cord as the two components of the central nervous system
items.what: The brain coordinates mental processes, behaviour, and bodily activity. The spinal cord is a cable of nerve tissue connecting the brain to the PNS via afferent (sensory) tracts that carry messages toward the brain and efferent (motor) tracts that carry messages away from the brain.
items.why: The brain and spinal cord are the processing and routing centre of all neural activity. Knowing the direction of information flow through each structure is essential for describing conscious responses and the spinal reflex.
items.example: When a person decides to pick up a cup, efferent tracts in the spinal cord carry the motor command from the brain down to the muscles of the hand and arm.

items.title: I can describe the role of the somatic nervous system and the neural pathways it contains
items.what: The somatic nervous system (SNS) is a division of the PNS that transmits neural messages related to voluntary motor movement. It contains sensory (afferent) neural pathways made up of sensory neurons that carry messages toward the CNS, and motor (efferent) neural pathways made up of motor neurons that carry messages from the CNS to skeletal muscles.
items.why: The somatic nervous system is the pathway for all voluntary, conscious actions and is directly involved in the spinal reflex. Correctly identifying its role and direction of transmission is a core exam skill.
items.example: A person reaching out to catch a ball uses the somatic nervous system: sensory neurons carry visual and tactile information to the CNS, and motor neurons carry the movement command to the skeletal muscles of the arm.

items.title: I can describe the role of the autonomic nervous system and distinguish between its sympathetic and parasympathetic subdivisions
items.what: The autonomic nervous system (ANS) is a division of the PNS that regulates visceral muscles, organs, and glands without conscious control. The sympathetic nervous system activates these structures to prepare the body for a threat or stressor. The parasympathetic nervous system maintains and restores optimal, balanced functioning of these structures.
items.why: The ANS controls the body's internal environment automatically, which explains unconscious physiological responses during stress and rest. Confusing the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions is one of the most common student errors in this topic.
items.example: During a frightening situation, the sympathetic nervous system increases heart rate and dilates pupils. After the threat passes, the parasympathetic nervous system slows the heart rate and restores normal digestion.

items.title: I can identify the three types of neurons and describe the direction in which each transmits neural messages
items.what: Sensory neurons (afferent) transmit messages about bodily sensations from the PNS to the CNS. Motor neurons (efferent) transmit messages about motor movement from the CNS to the PNS. Interneurons transfer messages between sensory and motor neurons and make up the brain and spinal cord.
items.why: Each neuron type has a specific directional role in the nervous system. Knowing which neuron type is found where — and which direction it transmits — is necessary for describing both conscious responses and the spinal reflex accurately.
items.example: In the spinal reflex: sensory neurons carry the pain signal from the skin to the spinal cord; interneurons in the spinal cord relay the signal; motor neurons carry the withdrawal command to the skeletal muscles.

items.title: I can compare the CNS and PNS in terms of the types of neurons each contains
items.what: The CNS — comprising the brain and spinal cord — is made up of interneurons. The PNS is made up of sensory (afferent) neurons and motor (efferent) neurons.
items.why: This comparison is tested directly in VCE multiple-choice and short-answer questions. Students frequently and incorrectly state that the spinal cord contains sensory or motor neurons rather than interneurons.
items.example: A question asks which neurons make up the spinal cord. The correct answer is interneurons, because the spinal cord is part of the CNS — not sensory or motor neurons, which belong to the PNS.

items.title: I can describe the five steps involved in a conscious response to a sensory stimulus, naming the divisions of the nervous system at each step
items.what: Step 1: Sensory receptors detect the stimulus. Step 2: The message travels via afferent pathways in the somatic nervous system and then the spinal cord to the brain (CNS). Step 3: The brain processes the information and initiates a voluntary motor response. Step 4: The motor message travels via efferent pathways in the spinal cord and then the somatic nervous system to skeletal muscles. Step 5: Skeletal muscles carry out the response.
items.why: This five-step pathway is the standard structure for exam questions asking students to describe how a conscious response is coordinated. Each step must name the correct division and direction of transmission.
items.example: Feeling cold water on the hand (step 1) leads the CNS to decide to turn on the hot tap (step 3), with skeletal muscles in the arm and hand carrying out the action (step 5) — all via the somatic nervous system and spinal cord.

subtopic.name: Conscious and Unconscious Responses
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how the divisions and subdivisions of the nervous system enable conscious responses — deliberate, voluntary actions initiated by the brain — and unconscious responses, including the physiological responses of the autonomic nervous system and the spinal reflex.
subtopic.why: Being able to identify and justify whether a response is conscious or unconscious, and naming the specific divisions involved, is one of the most frequently assessed skills in VCE Psychology. Precision with terminology and the direction of neural transmission is essential for full marks.

items.title: I can identify the key distinguishing characteristic between conscious and unconscious responses
items.what: Conscious responses are deliberate and voluntary, initiated with conscious awareness. Unconscious responses are automatic and involuntary, occurring without conscious awareness. The distinguishing feature is conscious awareness — not simply whether the brain is involved — because some unconscious responses involve the brain stem.
items.why: Students frequently make the error of saying unconscious responses do not involve the brain at all. The 2023 VCAA examiners' report specifically flagged this misconception. Using conscious awareness as the distinguishing feature avoids this error.
items.example: A scenario that says a person 'decides' to withdraw their hand indicates a conscious response. A scenario that says a person 'immediately' withdraws their hand indicates an unconscious response — the word choice signals the type.

subtopic.name: Conscious and Unconscious Responses
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how the divisions and subdivisions of the nervous system enable conscious responses — deliberate, voluntary actions initiated by the brain — and unconscious responses, including the physiological responses of the autonomic nervous system and the spinal reflex.
subtopic.why: Being able to identify and justify whether a response is conscious or unconscious, and naming the specific divisions involved, is one of the most frequently assessed skills in VCE Psychology. items.title: I can describe the specific physiological responses of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems
items.what: Sympathetic responses include increased heart rate, increased breathing rate, pupil dilation, activation of sweat glands, inhibition of digestion, bladder relaxation, secretion of adrenaline from adrenal glands, and increased glucose release. Parasympathetic responses are the reversal of these: steady heart rate, constricted lung airways, pupil constriction, regulated perspiration, normal digestion, controlled urination, no secretion of adrenaline, and reduced glucose release.
items.why: Individual sympathetic and parasympathetic responses are tested in multiple-choice questions that require students to correctly match the response to the division. Memorising specific examples is necessary.
items.example: A VCE exam question asks which response occurs when the sympathetic nervous system is dominant. Increased heart rate, dilated pupils, and inhibited digestion are all correct answers. Bladder constriction and normal digestion are parasympathetic responses and would be incorrect.

subtopic.name: Conscious and Unconscious Responses
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how the divisions and subdivisions of the nervous system enable conscious responses — deliberate, voluntary actions initiated by the brain — and unconscious responses, including the physiological responses of the autonomic nervous system and the spinal reflex.
subtopic.why: Being able to identify and justify whether a response is conscious or unconscious, and naming the specific divisions involved, is one of the most frequently assessed skills in VCE Psychology. items.title: I can explain the spinal reflex as an unconscious response, describing the four steps and the role of the reflex arc
items.what: Step 1: Sensory receptors detect a harmful stimulus and sensory neurons transmit the message via the somatic nervous system to the spinal cord. Step 2: An interneuron in the spinal cord relays the message from the sensory neuron to a motor neuron, initiating an automatic motor response independently of the brain. Step 3: Motor neurons transmit the message via the somatic nervous system to skeletal muscles, which carry out the response. Step 4: The sensory message continues to the brain, which registers the sensation after the response has already occurred. The reflex arc is the path the neural signal travels during this process.
items.why: The spinal reflex is faster than a conscious response because the signal travels only to the spinal cord rather than all the way to the brain. This adaptive advantage — responding to danger before conscious awareness — is a key exam concept.
items.example: Touching an extremely hot pan: the hand is withdrawn automatically (steps 1-3) before the person consciously registers the pain (step 4). The brain only becomes aware of the burn after the hand has already been pulled away.

items.title: I can compare conscious motor responses and the spinal reflex, identifying one similarity and one difference
items.what: Similarity: both involve afferent (sensory) neural pathways carrying messages toward the CNS and efferent (motor) neural pathways carrying messages to skeletal muscles via the somatic nervous system. Difference: conscious responses are initiated by the brain, whereas the spinal reflex is initiated by interneurons in the spinal cord independently of the brain.
items.why: This comparison is a standard exam question type in VCE Psychology. Students must use precise terminology about the pathway and initiating structure to receive full marks.
items.example: Both responses use motor neurons in the somatic nervous system to activate skeletal muscles. However, when a person consciously chooses to move their arm, the command originates in the brain; when a spinal reflex occurs, the command originates in the spinal cord without brain involvement in the initiation.

items.title: I can identify and describe the structures that make up the neural synapse
items.what: The neural synapse is the region comprising: the axon terminals of the presynaptic neuron (which contain synaptic vesicles that store neurochemicals), the synaptic gap (the space between the two neurons), and the dendrites of the postsynaptic neuron (which contain receptor sites — protein molecules that receive neurochemicals).
items.why: Each structure of the synapse has a specific function in transmission. Exam questions frequently ask students to name and describe these structures, or to correctly identify which neuron releases and which receives neurochemicals.
items.example: The presynaptic neuron releases glutamate from its axon terminals into the synaptic gap. The glutamate crosses the gap and binds to receptor sites on the dendrites of the postsynaptic neuron.

subtopic.name: The Neural Synapse and Synaptic Transmission
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structures that make up the neural synapse — including axon terminals, the synaptic gap, dendrites, and receptor sites — and the four-step process of synaptic transmission by which neurochemicals convey neural information from the presynaptic neuron to the postsynaptic neuron.
subtopic.why: The neural synapse and synaptic transmission are the structural and chemical basis of all neural communication. Understanding this process is necessary for explaining how neurotransmitters and neuromodulators produce their effects on brain functioning.

items.title: I can describe the four steps of synaptic transmission in order
items.what: Step 1: Neurochemicals are produced in the axon terminals of the presynaptic neuron. Step 2: Neurochemicals are released from the axon terminals into the synaptic gap. Step 3: Neurochemicals bind to their corresponding receptor sites on the dendrites of the postsynaptic neuron. Step 4: The neurochemical affects the postsynaptic neuron, either triggering or inhibiting a response.
items.why: This sequence is the foundation for describing how any specific neurochemical (glutamate, GABA, dopamine, or serotonin) exerts its effect. Exam questions that ask students to describe successful neural transmission expect this sequence to be referenced.
items.example: A three-mark exam question asks students to describe, with reference to glutamate, the process of successful synaptic transmission. The response must trace glutamate from production in the axon terminals, through release into the synaptic gap, to binding at receptor sites, to its excitatory effect on the postsynaptic neuron.

subtopic.name: The Neural Synapse and Synaptic Transmission
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structures that make up the neural synapse — including axon terminals, the synaptic gap, dendrites, and receptor sites — and the four-step process of synaptic transmission by which neurochemicals convey neural information from the presynaptic neuron to the postsynaptic neuron.
subtopic.why: The neural synapse and synaptic transmission are the structural and chemical basis of all neural communication. Understanding this process is necessary for explaining how neurotransmitters and neuromodulators produce their effects on brain functioning.

items.title: I can explain why each neurochemical can only bind to its corresponding receptor site
items.what: Each neurochemical has a distinct molecular structure that corresponds to only one specific receptor site. A neurochemical cannot bind to the receptor sites of other neurochemicals because their molecular structures do not match. This is known as receptor specificity.
items.why: Receptor specificity explains why different neurochemicals produce different effects and why neurochemical imbalances affect specific functions rather than all functions equally.
items.example: Glutamate can only bind to glutamate receptor sites. It cannot bind to GABA receptor sites, even though both are neurotransmitters present in the same neural synapse region. This is analogous to a key that only fits one specific lock.

subtopic.name: The Neural Synapse and Synaptic Transmission
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the structures that make up the neural synapse — including axon terminals, the synaptic gap, dendrites, and receptor sites — and the four-step process of synaptic transmission by which neurochemicals convey neural information from the presynaptic neuron to the postsynaptic neuron.
subtopic.why: The neural synapse and synaptic transmission are the structural and chemical basis of all neural communication. Understanding this process is necessary for explaining how neurotransmitters and neuromodulators produce their effects on brain functioning.

items.title: I can compare neurotransmitters and neuromodulators in terms of scale, speed, and duration of effect
items.what: Neurotransmitters affect one or two postsynaptic neurons and enable rapid, localised communication across a single synapse. Neuromodulators affect multiple postsynaptic neurons across larger areas of brain tissue and produce slower, more long-lasting effects. Both must bind to specific receptor sites to have their effects.
items.why: This comparison is a direct exam requirement. Confusing neurotransmitters with neuromodulators — or incorrectly stating that neuromodulators affect only one neuron — is a common error that costs marks.
items.example: Glutamate (a neurotransmitter) rapidly activates one postsynaptic neuron at a specific synapse. Dopamine (a neuromodulator) is released into multiple synapses and influences widespread areas of the brain over a longer time period.

subtopic.name: Neurotransmitters and Neuromodulators
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the distinction between neurotransmitters (which affect one or two postsynaptic neurons) and neuromodulators (which affect multiple postsynaptic neurons across wider brain areas), and the specific roles of glutamate, GABA, dopamine, and serotonin in neural functioning.
subtopic.why: These four neurochemicals are explicitly named in the VCE study design and appear in almost every exam. Understanding what each one does — and how imbalances relate to conditions such as epilepsy, depression, anxiety, and addiction — is essential for apply-and-analyse questions.

items.title: I can describe excitatory and inhibitory effects at the postsynaptic neuron and explain that neither effect is guaranteed
items.what: An excitatory effect increases the likelihood of the postsynaptic neuron firing an action potential. An inhibitory effect decreases this likelihood. Importantly, these effects only change the probability of firing — they do not guarantee that the neuron will or will not fire an action potential.
items.why: Students frequently state that excitatory neurotransmitters cause the postsynaptic neuron to fire, or that inhibitory neurotransmitters prevent it from firing. The correct language is that they increase or decrease the likelihood of firing.
items.example: When glutamate binds to its receptor sites, it increases the likelihood that the postsynaptic neuron will fire an action potential — but firing is not guaranteed. When GABA binds, it decreases this likelihood — but the neuron is not guaranteed to remain silent.

subtopic.name: Neurotransmitters and Neuromodulators

subtopic.why: These four neurochemicals are explicitly named in the VCE study design and appear in almost every exam. Understanding what each one does — and how imbalances relate to conditions such as epilepsy, depression, anxiety, and addiction — is essential for apply-and-analyse questions.

items.title: I can describe the role of glutamate as the main excitatory neurotransmitter, including its role in learning and memory
items.what: Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter in the nervous system. It increases the likelihood of the postsynaptic neuron firing an action potential. Its excitatory effects form and strengthen synaptic connections between neurons that are repeatedly activated during learning, enabling synaptic plasticity, learning, memory, thought, and movement.
items.why: Glutamate connects the neurotransmitter content directly to synaptic plasticity in lesson 2D. Exam questions on long-term potentiation frequently require students to reference the role of glutamate in structural changes at the synapse.
items.example: Each time a student practises a new piano piece, glutamate is released at the relevant synapses. Over repeated practice sessions, its excitatory effects strengthen those synaptic connections, making the piece progressively easier to play from memory.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the distinction between neurotransmitters (which affect one or two postsynaptic neurons) and neuromodulators (which affect multiple postsynaptic neurons across wider brain areas), and the specific roles of glutamate, GABA, dopamine, and serotonin in neural functioning.
subtopic.why: These four neurochemicals are explicitly named in the VCE study design and appear in almost every exam. Understanding what each one does — and how imbalances relate to conditions such as epilepsy, depression, anxiety, and addiction — is essential for apply-and-analyse questions.

items.title: I can describe the role of GABA as the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, including its role in anxiety and seizures
items.what: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. It decreases the likelihood of the postsynaptic neuron firing an action potential, preventing the overexcitation of neurons. A deficiency of GABA is associated with increased anxiety and epileptic seizures, because excitatory neural signals are not adequately suppressed.
items.why: GABA's inhibitory role is directly applied in exam scenarios involving anxiety disorders and epilepsy. Students must correctly classify GABA as inhibitory and explain how a deficiency — not an excess — causes these conditions.
items.example: A person diagnosed with epilepsy likely has a deficiency of GABA. Without sufficient GABA to suppress excitatory signals, neurons fire uncontrollably, producing a seizure. Medication that increases GABA activity can reduce the frequency of seizures.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the distinction between neurotransmitters (which affect one or two postsynaptic neurons) and neuromodulators (which affect multiple postsynaptic neurons across wider brain areas), and the specific roles of glutamate, GABA, dopamine, and serotonin in neural functioning.
subtopic.why: These four neurochemicals are explicitly named in the VCE study design and appear in almost every exam. Understanding what each one does — and how imbalances relate to conditions such as epilepsy, depression, anxiety, and addiction — is essential for apply-and-analyse questions.

items.title: I can explain why both excitatory and inhibitory effects are necessary for optimal brain functioning
items.what: Optimal brain functioning requires a balance between excitatory and inhibitory effects. Without GABA counterbalancing glutamate, neurons would fire uncontrollably, causing anxiety and seizures. Without glutamate counterbalancing GABA, neurons would be insufficiently activated, causing learning difficulties, poor concentration, and mental exhaustion.
items.why: Students frequently assume inhibitory effects are negative because they reduce neural activity. Exam questions that ask students to evaluate whether inhibitory effects are harmful require this balanced understanding.
items.example: A student with very low glutamate and high GABA activity might find it very difficult to form new memories or concentrate, because the excitatory activation needed to strengthen synaptic connections during learning is insufficient.

subtopic.why: These four neurochemicals are explicitly named in the VCE study design and appear in almost every exam. Understanding what each one does — and how imbalances relate to conditions such as epilepsy, depression, anxiety, and addiction — is essential for apply-and-analyse questions.

items.title: I can describe the roles of dopamine as a neuromodulator, including its pathways in the brain
items.what: Dopamine is a neuromodulator primarily responsible for voluntary motor movement, the experience of pleasure, and reward-based learning. Dopamine originating from the substantia nigra (midbrain) coordinates smooth, voluntary motor movement. Dopamine originating from the ventral tegmental area (midbrain) is associated with pleasure and reward-based learning. Dopamine can have both excitatory and inhibitory effects depending on the receptor site.
items.why: Dopamine's dual roles in motor control and reward explain both Parkinson's disease (motor symptoms from loss of substantia nigra neurons) and addiction (repeated reward-triggered dopamine release motivates behaviour repetition). Both are common exam application contexts.
items.example: When a person wins money gambling, dopamine is released from the ventral tegmental area, producing a pleasurable sensation. This motivates the person to gamble again to recreate the experience, which is the neurochemical basis of gambling addiction.

subtopic.why: These four neurochemicals are explicitly named in the VCE study design and appear in almost every exam. Understanding what each one does — and how imbalances relate to conditions such as epilepsy, depression, anxiety, and addiction — is essential for apply-and-analyse questions.

items.title: I can describe the roles of serotonin as a neuromodulator, including its effects on mood and the sleep-wake cycle
items.what: Serotonin is a neuromodulator primarily responsible for mood regulation and the sleep-wake cycle. It originates from the raphe nuclei in the brainstem and has inhibitory effects on the postsynaptic neuron. Appropriate serotonin levels support positive, stable moods. Low serotonin levels are associated with depression. Serotonin also influences appetite, digestion, and arousal.
items.why: Serotonin's role in depression explains why many antidepressant medications work by increasing serotonin levels or targeting serotonin receptor sites. This clinical application is tested directly in VCE exam scenarios.
items.example: A 65-year-old woman presenting with persistent low mood, reduced interest in daily activities, and difficulty getting out of bed may have low serotonin levels. A doctor may prescribe medication that increases serotonin availability in the brain to stabilise and improve mood.

items.title: I can define synaptic plasticity and explain its relationship to learning and memory
items.what: Synaptic plasticity is the ability of synaptic connections to change over time in response to activity or experience. It is the fundamental mechanism of memory formation that leads to learning. When experiences cause neurons to coactivate, their synaptic connections physically change, forming memory traces — neural pathways that represent what has been learnt.
items.why: This definition is precise and must be stated accurately in exam responses. A common error is defining synaptic plasticity as the ability of the brain (rather than synaptic connections specifically) to change — this wording loses marks.
items.example: A student practising multiplication tables each day causes the neurons involved in that knowledge to coactivate repeatedly. Their synaptic connections strengthen over time, forming a memory trace that makes recall faster and more reliable.

subtopic.name: Synaptic Plasticity and Learning
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers synaptic plasticity as the ability of synaptic connections to change over time in response to activity or experience, including the three mechanisms — sprouting, rerouting, and pruning — and the two forms of plasticity underlying learning and memory: long-term potentiation and long-term depression.
subtopic.why: Synaptic plasticity is the neurological explanation for how learning and memory occur. It connects directly to the neurotransmitter content from lesson 2C — particularly glutamate's role — and is assessed through both recall and complex application questions involving realistic learning scenarios.

items.title: I can explain sprouting as a mechanism of synaptic plasticity
items.what: Sprouting is the ability of dendrites or axons to develop new extensions or branches. This increases the reach of the neuron and enables the formation of new synaptic connections with other neurons.
items.why: Sprouting is the structural mechanism behind the formation of new synaptic connections during learning and recovery from brain injury. It appears as one of the structural changes listed under long-term potentiation in exam responses.
items.example: When a person learns a new skill such as knitting, sprouting in the relevant brain regions allows dendritic branches to extend and form new connections with neighbouring neurons, expanding the neural pathway associated with that skill.

subtopic.name: Synaptic Plasticity and Learning
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers synaptic plasticity as the ability of synaptic connections to change over time in response to activity or experience, including the three mechanisms — sprouting, rerouting, and pruning — and the two forms of plasticity underlying learning and memory: long-term potentiation and long-term depression.
subtopic.why: Synaptic plasticity is the neurological explanation for how learning and memory occur. It connects directly to the neurotransmitter content from lesson 2C — particularly glutamate's role — and is assessed through both recall and complex application questions involving realistic learning scenarios.

items.title: I can explain rerouting as a mechanism of synaptic plasticity
items.what: Rerouting is the ability of a neuron connected to a damaged neuron to abandon that connection and form a new synaptic connection with an undamaged neuron instead. This reestablishes the synaptic connection via an alternative route, restoring brain functioning.
items.why: Rerouting explains how the brain can partially recover function after injury by finding alternative neural pathways. It is distinct from sprouting (which forms entirely new connections) and pruning (which removes connections).
items.example: After a stroke damages neurons in a motor pathway, rerouting may allow neighbouring undamaged neurons to form alternative connections that partially restore the ability to move the affected limb over weeks of rehabilitation.

subtopic.name: Synaptic Plasticity and Learning
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers synaptic plasticity as the ability of synaptic connections to change over time in response to activity or experience, including the three mechanisms — sprouting, rerouting, and pruning — and the two forms of plasticity underlying learning and memory: long-term potentiation and long-term depression.
subtopic.why: Synaptic plasticity is the neurological explanation for how learning and memory occur. It connects directly to the neurotransmitter content from lesson 2C — particularly glutamate's role — and is assessed through both recall and complex application questions involving realistic learning scenarios.

items.title: I can explain pruning as a mechanism of synaptic plasticity
items.what: Pruning is the elimination of synaptic connections that are not adequately activated. When synaptic connections are not used, they are removed to accommodate stronger and more essential connections, enhancing the efficiency of brain functioning.
items.why: Students frequently assume pruning is harmful because it removes connections. The correct understanding is that pruning is adaptive — it frees neural resources for connections that are used more frequently, improving overall brain efficiency.
items.example: A person who learnt to play the recorder in primary school but has not played for 15 years will find that those synaptic connections have been pruned, making the skill harder to perform. The brain allocated those resources to more frequently used pathways.

subtopic.name: Synaptic Plasticity and Learning
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers synaptic plasticity as the ability of synaptic connections to change over time in response to activity or experience, including the three mechanisms — sprouting, rerouting, and pruning — and the two forms of plasticity underlying learning and memory: long-term potentiation and long-term depression.
subtopic.why: Synaptic plasticity is the neurological explanation for how learning and memory occur. It connects directly to the neurotransmitter content from lesson 2C — particularly glutamate's role — and is assessed through both recall and complex application questions involving realistic learning scenarios.

items.title: I can explain long-term potentiation, including the structural changes it produces at the neural synapse
items.what: Long-term potentiation (LTP) is the long-lasting, experience-dependent strengthening of synaptic connections that are regularly coactivated. Repeated high-intensity stimulation of the postsynaptic neuron — driven by increased glutamate release — produces three structural changes: an increased number of receptor sites on the postsynaptic neuron's dendrites, bushier dendrites due to sprouting, and an increased number of synaptic connections due to sprouting.
items.why: LTP is the neurological mechanism of learning — it explains why practice makes performance faster and more efficient. Exam questions require students to name and describe the specific structural changes, not just state that connections strengthen.
items.example: A person learning to type using a new keyboard layout practises daily for two months. LTP in the relevant neural pathways increases the number of receptor sites and produces bushier dendrites, making the pathway more efficient and typing progressively faster and more accurate.

subtopic.name: Synaptic Plasticity and Learning
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers synaptic plasticity as the ability of synaptic connections to change over time in response to activity or experience, including the three mechanisms — sprouting, rerouting, and pruning — and the two forms of plasticity underlying learning and memory: long-term potentiation and long-term depression.
subtopic.why: Synaptic plasticity is the neurological explanation for how learning and memory occur. It connects directly to the neurotransmitter content from lesson 2C — particularly glutamate's role — and is assessed through both recall and complex application questions involving realistic learning scenarios.

items.title: I can explain long-term depression, including the structural changes it produces at the neural synapse
items.what: Long-term depression (LTD) is the long-lasting, experience-dependent weakening of synaptic connections between neurons that are not regularly coactivated. Infrequent, low-intensity stimulation of the postsynaptic neuron produces three structural changes: a decreased number of receptor sites on the postsynaptic neuron's dendrites, fewer dendrites due to pruning, and a decreased number of synaptic connections due to pruning.
items.why: LTD is adaptive — it prevents the brain from maintaining unnecessary connections and frees resources for more relevant memory traces. It also explains forgetting and skill loss after periods of disuse.
items.example: A student who studied Indonesian in Year 8 but stopped practising for five years experiences LTD in the relevant neural pathways: receptor sites are reduced, dendrites are pruned, and the connections weaken — making Indonesian vocabulary increasingly difficult to recall.

items.title: I can compare long-term potentiation and long-term depression, identifying one similarity and one difference
items.what: Similarity: both LTP and LTD are long-lasting, experience-dependent forms of synaptic plasticity that involve structural changes to the neural synapse. Difference: LTP results from frequent coactivation and strengthens synaptic connections (involving sprouting), whereas LTD results from infrequent coactivation and weakens synaptic connections (involving pruning).
items.why: Comparing LTP and LTD is a standard exam question type. Students must use the precise terms 'strengthening' and 'weakening' rather than informal language, and must link each process to the correct mechanism.
items.example: A musician who practises daily experiences LTP in the relevant motor pathways (connections strengthen via sprouting). If they stop practising for a year, LTD weakens those same connections via pruning. Resuming practice can restrengthen the connections through LTP again.

items.title: I can apply long-term potentiation and long-term depression to a novel learning scenario
items.what: LTP occurs when a person regularly practises or uses a skill or knowledge, causing the relevant synaptic connections to strengthen and the neural pathway to become more efficient. LTD occurs when a previously learned skill or knowledge is no longer regularly used, causing those synaptic connections to weaken and become less efficient.
items.why: VCE exam questions routinely present a new scenario — such as a person learning a sport, instrument, or work skill — and ask students to explain the role of LTP and/or LTD. Applying the concepts to an unfamiliar context is the highest-level skill tested.
items.example: Duncan's employees learn a new typing method over two months (LTP: the neural pathways for the new method are repeatedly coactivated, strengthening those connections). Simultaneously, LTD weakens the old typing method's neural pathway because it is no longer being regularly used, helping employees abandon the old habit.
